FLORENCE, Italy Sept. 12.—When
Frederic Cerboni was discovered
recently, several short paragraphs
were published about him. He is
a chemist by profession and is 90
years old. When he declared that he
expects to live twice that age, people were
surprised. They were more surprised
when he was reported as saying that
the secret of health and long life was
to avoid soap and water and never
wash himself. According to the
statements then published, he has never
taken a bath.


It now appears that these statements
are all true. For the editor of La
Nazione of this city sent a special cor-
respondent to the aged professor's
home at Gelsomino, not far from Rome,
and interviewed him.


Before the interview was published
the professor read it over and then
signed it. Here is a brief of what he
says in it: The secret of long life and
health is to get as close to
nature as possible. Go back
to the history of the beginning of
all things. Did not Adam and Eve and
Moses and Aaron and Methuselah and
the hosts that lived in the first cen-
turies live to great old ages? They
were close to nature. They did not use
soaps and toilet powder and all the
abominable things people nowadays
use. In the Roman period, the luxuries
were the baths. A man
in those days was old at 81. In the
middle ages where do you find baths,
looking glasses, brushes, sponges,
soaps? It is true that disease wiped
out the people freely, but that was be-
cause they had no physicians worthy
of the name and no knowledge of the
science of cure.


"The present day hygiene—what is it?
A myth, mere superstition. Microbes
are killed by other microbes. That is
the long and short of it. I am a chem-
ist, I know my profession well and
therefore, I know all about this fad of
hygiene.


Look at the number of people who
live to 100 or more. The newspapers
tell us of them now and again. Who
are they? Simple peasants on the moun-
tains or in the country. They do not take
daily baths or use the deadly soaps and
toilet foolishnesses. They live close
to nature and the soil from which they
sprung.


To wash one's clothes or one's rooms
is a different matter. I am hale and hearty,
I have a good appetite. I sleep well.
I am vigorous and in my prime. I have
never had a day's illness in my life."

Washington, Aug 23.—Let nobody make the mistake of supposing that the political campaign this year is "a dollar limit game just because both congressional committees have asked for dollar contributions to their campaign funds. The dollar contributions are very acceptable at the headquarters of both committees, but the indications now are that if some more substantial donations are not made, the committees will find themselves seriously embarrassed before election day."

This was the summary made to-day of the financial condition of the committees of the Republican and Democratic parties by a politician in close touch with the campaign.

"The campaign this year," he continued, "will require considerable money on both sides and unless it should be forthcoming there may be a practical putting up of the political shutters. As a matter of fact, both campaign committees expect to receive some good contributions this year, as in the past, and are not depending absolutely on the dollar subscriptions. the battle, it suffices to say that he was
abandoned almost at the outset of his great
task in Canada by Melbourne and his col
leagues for at most an error of judgment
which easily could have been rectified. He
was abandoned in submission to the over
bearing attitude of so reckless an assailant
as Brougham. By every consideration of
loyalty Melbourne and his colleagues ought
to have thrown the whole weight and pro-
tection of his Cabinet around a Governor
General who had been intrusted by the
Crown with extraordinary powers. But
Lord Melbourne had to choose between the
disapproval of the House of Lords and the
abandonment of Lord Durham. He elected
to disallow the ordinance rather than risk
a hostile vote.


The news of the disallowance of his
ordinance caused Durham to resign his
office, but not until he had published the
so-called Act of Indemnity, which on the
score of a minor technical error had con-
demned his treatment of Canadian pris-
oners. But, as John Stuart Mill pointed
out at the time, Durham, though he had been
thwarted by Brougham, had not failed.
The period of Durham's government was
but of five months duration, yet in that
short time he brought about vast political
results. His policy it was that pacified
Canada and secured its retention. He saw
the defects of the existing legislation and
devised the remedy. In the report which
he presented to Parliament after his return
to England he propounded a scheme for the
future government of Canada which was
destined to be adopted in the end, the union
of Upper and Lower Canada. This union,
accomplished in 1841, led to the formation
of the Dominion in 1867. His projects of
state aided emigration and of an inter-
colonial railway have been carried out.
We observe, finally, that his proposal to
make the Canadian Executive responsible
to the United Legislature and to grant the
latter the most complete constitutional
privileges has been embodied in the organic
law of the Dominion. Of Durham it may
truthfully be said that the free institutions
now enjoyed by the Canadians are due
primarily to the deep impression made by
his report to Parliament.


The royal assent to a bill for the govern
ment of Canada, based on his proposals,
was given on July 7, 1841, five days be-
fore Lord Durham's death. He had been
conscious, even in the darkest hour of
his life, that his work would stand, and
that no matter what men said at the moment
he had served England and her scattered
children well. He went to his grave a
great but temporarily discredited man.
Yet he had no misgivings. He was con-
tent to await the verdict of history, the
triumph which he foresaw of his policy
in Canada, and the acceptance of the prin-
ciples of government on which he had
based his political reputation in his Re-
port on the Affairs of British North America.
He never doubted that coming genera
tions would recognize the honesty of his
intentions and the magnitude of his achieve
ment. It may well be, as his biographer
says, that the Lambton motto, "lie jour
viendra," flashed through his mind as he
murmured when dying, "Canada will one
day do justice to my memory." From
Bulwer Lytton's tribute to Durham, which
is reproduced in the book before us, we
quote these lines:


Courts may have known, than thee, O reader too;
States may have found, than thine, O subtle brain;
But States shall honor many a formal fool.


And many tawdry favour courts may gain,
Ere King or People in their need shall see


A soul so grand as that which went with thee.

HARRISBURG, July 5-The State
game commission held its semi annual
meeting at its new Office in the new
capitol today, for the purpose of hear
ing the semi-annual report of Secre-
tar1 Kalbfus and the transaction 'of
routine business. There were present
President James II. Worden, Harris
burg: secretary, Joseph Kalbfus, Har-
risburg J. NJ. Phillips, Pittsburg; c..
X Sober, Lcwisburg; William Hey
ward Meyers, Williamsport;. ;.EDr.
Charles b. Peurose, Philadelphia, and
former State Treasurer Frank c.
Harris. of Clearfeld.


\ most encouraging condition of
affairs regarding the increase of game
in the State was presented by SeCrc-
tary Kalbfus, which is mainly due to
the enforcement of the laws and the
great interest the public is taking in
game protection. The absence of forest
fires has also tended to increase game,
and DR. Kalbfus commends the vigil
ance of the authorities in this direc-
tion.


Attention j. called to the fact that
the game laws in some respects are un-
fair, and their repeal is recommended.


For instance a gunner in this State
can only kill certain number of
migratory fowl, but in adjoining
States to which they fly when leaving
Pennsylvania the gunners can kill as
many "a they please. There is also
law in this State providing a fine of
$50 for digging a rabbit out of its war
rem. while the fine for shooting a rab-
bit is but $40, and DR.. Kalbfus wants
to know wherein lies the difference.
Again, the law imposes a fine of $50
for destroying a birds nest on a tree,
and yet the owner of a home, if he
finds robins or other birds destroying
his fruit or damaging his property can
kill them indiscriminately, and there
is no fine at all.


Secretary Kalbfus strongly recon-
mends that a law be passed making it
a penal offence for any unnaturaIized
foreign born resident TO own a gun or
any other kind Of firearms. In the last
six months five officers of the game
commission, in hunting offenders
against the game laws, have been shot
at and wounded by foreigners, and one
man was brutally murdered by Italians
in the western part of the State, and
his. body thrown into the river simply
because he performed his duty and
prosecuted foreign violators of the
game laws


The game wardens, by the way. are
all doing good work, and have pros
ecuted many offenders, the fines from
which 20 10 the department.


The department brought from Ala,
bama for propagating purposes, 3, 547
quail. and they are all said to be doing
finely. A number died on the way
here, but in bringing quail here next
year DR.. Kalbfus will have them ship
ped in a patent box which will admit
Of them getting light, air, food and
water. Three sites foI game preserves
have been selected, one in Clinton
county, a second in Clearfield and
third in Franklin, all on forestry land

The members of the state board of
! railroad commissioners at their regu-
lar monthly meeting at the headquar-
ters of the commission in Sioux Falls
| decided that Frank LeCocq, chairman

will be held in the Office Of the son of
Senator Thomas c. Platt, and the tes-
timony taken there will become part
! of the record in the case now pending
In the federal court


The case arises from a complaint
| filed with the railroad commissioners
| by the Aberdeen Is. d. National bank
last July. The complaint asked that
| the United States Express company's
Office at Aberdeen be required to ex-
tend its hours for receiving shipments
OF cash for transportation over it's
lines. The railroad commissioners,
, after hearing in the case, decided in
favor OF the bank and issued an order
requiring the express company to re-
ceive shipments of currency at any
hour during the day


The express company appealed from
the order of the board to the United
States court, where Judge Garland is
sued writ temporarily enioining the
board from enforcing it's order. The
express company maintained that the
railroad commissioners have no iuris.
dictiOn over the acts of the company,
and that the order of the board was
unreasonable The commission has
since filed cross bill which asks the
federal court to compel the obedience
of the express company to the order of
the commission. The case, when de-
cided, is expected to establish a pre-
cedent as to the jurisdiction of boards
of railroad commissioners over ex.
press companies, and for this reason
the express company is cOntesting the

The members of the state board of railroad commissioners at their regular monthly meeting at the headquarters of the commission in Sioux Falls decided that Frank LeCocq, chairman of the board, and P. J. Rogde, legal adviser, should represent the board at a hearing to be held next Tuesday in New York city, in a case originating from an order of the board, and which now is pending in the United States court for South Dakota. The case arises from a complaint filed with the railroad commissioners by the Aberdeen Is. d. National bank last July. The complaint asked that the United States Express company's office at Aberdeen be required to extend its hours for receiving shipments of cash for transportation over its lines. The express company appealed from the order of the board to the United States court, where Judge Garland has issued writ temporarily enjoining the board from enforcing its order. The commission has since filed cross bill which asks the federal court to compel the obedience of the express company to the order of the commission. Ornaments, however, have their use, and very real use, in the house, and that is to add to the beauty of the interior. It is an unfortunate chance that gives to most new householders a very miscellaneous collection of ornaments acquired as wedding gifts. Well meant as many of these offerings are, they are chosen, in most cases, without the slightest regard to their future location or utilization. Terrible as it is to think of many of these objects, it is much more reassuring that the outlook is by no means so dark as it once was. The standards of good taste have risen markedly in America in the last twenty-five years, and the movement is still upward. The opportunities to purchase ugly ornaments—as if an ornament were no longer so numerous as formerly—are less. Better things are made and more of them. The individual maker, who is often an artist in quite true sense, has entered the field of commerce, and many beautiful and artistic ornamental objects can now be purchased almost everywhere.

The acquired ornaments of the home are the direct manifestations of the owner's taste, and show, in thoroughly unmistakable way, how far one has progressed in personal art culture. Perhaps this aspect of ornaments is seldom thought of, and perhaps it is of no special value; for the whole home is a unit. A home that contains ugly furniture and unsatisfactory curtains will not be redeemed by a beautiful vase or an exquisitely turned candlestick, admirable as each may be.

The lesser arts are entering the home more and more each day. The personal note of the individual craftsman is seen in many objects which, not long since, could only be obtained in factory-made form or not at all. But only beginning has been made, and vulgar art still flourishes amazingly. The prices of individual or exclusive designs, as they are sometimes called, is high, for the labor expended in their production is costly and the markets are somewhat restricted.

Glass, pottery and metal, to name the materials of which ornamental objects are chiefly made, are much more used in the house than formerly. And not only are they more used, but they are used in better way, with more intelligence and in more artistic forms. It is a good sign of the broadening influence of art that this is so. And it is a good sign that many people now appreciate and treasure such objects that not long since, scarcely knew them by name.

With this increased use comes greater responsibility. It is not sufficient simply to have objects; one must know how to use them and get the best from them. The arrangement of ornamental objects is quite as important as their possession, perhaps more so; for the most beautiful object loses much of its value if it is improperly disposed, or so placed that its fullest value is not given to the room in which it stands. Over-crowding with ornaments is an atrocity that should be avoided at all costs. Too many ornaments is distinctly worse than none at all. No ornaments show want of taste, failure to realize to the utmost the possibility of room decoration, and an ignorance of the refinements of life. Too many ornaments show lack of proportion and amount to vulgar overlooking of the rooms, which is even more disheartening than none at all. Of few things is it truer than that too much of a good thing may be bad.

Cobbler of Flanders.

It will be enforced by the Interstate Commerce Commission. According to the new law the roads were to have filed with the commission by midnight, all their tariffs and charges, showing not only the cost of transportation from point to point, but also what items go to the making up of the cost. to feed the great saws which snip them
into two and one-half foot lengths as
easily as though they were so many


split by another saw into thin strips
which are in turn converted into long
thin square strips by gang saws. Dell
hands toss these strips on a revolving
drum, which bears them against sun-
other saws and turns them out in the
form of oblong blocks.


Falling off to a moving belt the
blocks are whirled away to further
lathes. If the blocks are to be-
come nail handles, they are bored and
turned in most ingenious fashion at
high rate of speed; if they are desti-
ned for clothespins, the boring is, of course
dispensed with, and they are simply
turned into the desired shape.


From the lathes a belt conveys the
clothespins to a slotter, which rap-
idly cuts the slot. The pins emerge
with two symmetrical legs and are
swiftly borne by still a third belt to
the upper floor, where they and
nail handles are dried in vast heaps
at a high temperature in the dry room,
bleached with sulphur and finally pol-
ished in a revolving drum. Thence they descend again to
the packers, where they receive a ma-
ll inspection, and all the pins that are
not rejected are packed in boxes la-
beled "A" or "B," according to quality.


The rate of production is amazing
yet few are injured in the making;
nearly every pin and handle emerges
after its tortuous journey in perfect,
polished form.—New York Tribune.

Boston, May 21.—In a magnificent race which was fought desperately in each by inch from start to finish and which was rowed under favorable conditions both as to the wind and water, the Cornell Varsity eight-oared crew defeated the Harvard Varsity eight on the Charles river this afternoon by three lengths. The event, which was the concluding feature of an interesting regatta, was termed by rowing experts as a splendid exhibition of ideal racing by two carefully trained and finely balanced sets of oarsmen, taking into consideration the adverse conditions of the wind and a heavy swell left by pleasure boats which the police had failed to clear from the course. Cornell's official time over the course of 1 5/16 miles was 10 min. 35 secs., while Harvard crossed the finish in 10 min. and 42 seconds flat. The VARSITY race was preceded by an eight-oared race between crews from the Cascadilla preparatory School at Ithaca, N. Y. and the St. Paul preparatory school of this city, an event which was won by the former crew in 10 min. 18 1/2 secs. The course was 1 5/16 miles and Cascadilla won by five lengths after an exciting struggle. Another event was the single Scull contest between Harvard men competing for the Carroll cup and this was won by L. R. Smith of the Law School who also was the victor in the last year's contest for the Carroll trophy.

The big event of the day was witnessed by several thousand people who assembled at points of vantage on Harvard bridge, under which the Varsity rowed, on the Boston Sea wall and at a large grandstand at the Union Boat Club where the Varsity race finished. An early morning's placid river changed in the afternoon to rough surface, kicked up by an easterly breeze which ran up the river against the tide. The officials decided to run off the Varsity event, however, which was started about 8:01 P. M. The course was downstream with the tide and against the wind. The crews were given a flying start and both eight caught the water at the same moment. Both Harvard and Cornell showed skill in getting away, rowing in slow quarter stroke, then half and then a three-quarter with the broad fun stroke, each reached steadily and powerfully. Then Cornell hit a stroke of 36 at once while Harvard followed with 34. The shells were very close together, almost within striking distance it seemed. F. T. Bangs of New York remarked that Cornell evaded who had a mid course to veer off, and the danger of an accident was averted. The crews held even until the quarter mile, then Cornell forged slightly in the lead until she was a full half length ahead. At that time both shells were moving easily without the slightest hang, and both boats were well spaced.

At the half when Cornell was rowing 30 and Harvard 28 strokes faster in the minute, the Ithacans had increased their head to one length. At this point both crews began to fight the rough water. While the swell from the spectator's crafts began to bother the oarsmen badly, Harvard being nearer to the middle of the river, got a little the worst of the choppy water and the wake left in the pleasure boats. Neither the Cambridge oarsmen pulled a strong distance, killing stroke, watching the race from the grandstand. The coach of the Harvard eight saw with immense satisfaction that his pupil was practicing the quick catch of the water as the men pushed in. A feat for which he had been laboring from the first moment of his coaching. There was a snap at the beginning of the stroke while each was steady and sure. For her part Cornell exhibited Coach Courtney's slow steady stroke which with an eighth more vigorous working in perfect harmony, caused the Cornell shell fairly to bound through the water.

The Cornell method proved itself a thing of value, for at the three-quarter mile the Ithacans were one and one-quarter lengths ahead of the Harvard rower; Cornell did this with the stroke of 38 when Harvard was rowing at 34. Gradually the gain was increased and at the mile flag Cornell led by a length and a half. After this the Cornell men began to squirt in stroke, was pushed up to 42 and 50 was held to the very finish. Coxswain of Harvard took his cue from his Cornell competitor and increased the Crimson's stroke to 50.

The Harvard eight responded marvellously and after leaving the one and one-half mile station where the Ithacans led by two and a half lengths, striving as hard as she could, Cornell could not increase her lead by more than half a boat length. Enthusiastic cheers went up from all sides as the two shells flashed down to the finish line and there was a great demonstration as the Cornell oarsmen speeded past the finish flag, the victors in a thrilling race, after a desperate finish by three lengths of their shell. The Harvard men were given an ovation as they rowed by the finish flag, still in good form and apparently ready for another contest.

No saner, more conservative or thoughtful exposition of democratic faith could have been made than Mr. Bryan uttered at Madison Square Garden. Firebrand programs were all absent. Even such radical theories as public ownership of railroads and tariff revision were preached with the conservatism of a student, the defense of the theory in the one case being presented with the admission that the people are probably not ready for public ownership of railroads at this time and in the other case that tariff revision would not necessarily destroy the trusts. He adopts the Roosevelt view that corporations must not dominate politics or contribute to campaign funds. Owing to the digging of the Panama canal especial interest is now entertained regarding the early history of the Spanish main or the mainland as distinguished from the Islands of the coast found by the early Spanish navigators. "The town is all gone now" says the author, saving the cathedral tower, where the sweet Spanish bells once chimed and the little stone bridge, worn by so many mules' hoofs. There is dense tropical forest over the site of it, though the foundations of several houses may be traced, and two or three walls still stand, with brilliant creepers covering up the carved work. It is not an easy place to reach, for it is some six miles from new Panama, and the way lies through such tangle of creepers, over such swampy ground, poisonous with so many snakes, that it is little visited. It can be reached by sea on a fine day at high tide if the surf be not too boisterous. To landward of the present Panama there is a fine hill, called Mount Ancon. A little to the east there is a roll of highland, now fruitful market-garden or farm of orchards. This highland, some five or six miles from the ruins, is known as Buccaneers Hill. It was from the summit of this highland that the pirates first saw the city steeple. Volunteers were called for, and some of the men, more venturesome than the rest, climbed down on a ladder and with a large stick killed the snake. The horse was then lifted from the cistern and a veterinary surgeon applied antidotes for the snake's bite. Although the horse suffered considerably from the combined effects of the fall and the snake bites, it will recover.

Dallas, Feb. 28.--At the meeting of
State Prohibitionists the recommended
motion for the executive committee that
the members enter the Democratic
party was withdrawn, and substitute
motion to remain as an organization

for the committee to succeed W. A.
Bourland and W. P. Bailey, both of
Dallas.

found much that commends itself to her to-
day in their domestic arts and industries.


This has sent her searching in dark
attics, old closets and trunks to find neglected
and despised household stores that were
once the delight and pride of the housewife
of former days, and has brought about
revival of the homely occupations of a cen-
tury ago, for the handicraft of our grand-
mothers and their grandmothers is now
thought to have sufficient artistic value to
allow it to demand an honored place in
modern homes.


The household industries that have ex-
cited the most ardent admiration of the wo-
man of today, and upon which she has
eagerly seized for their decorative effect, are
the patchwork quilts and the old blue and
white homespun coverlets, the accumulation
of which delighted the soul of the housewife
of yesterday.


In themselves possessing a quaint and pe-
culiar charm, their artistic value is much
enhanced when placed, as they should be,
among harmonious surroundings—the fur-
niture of the colonial and revolutionary period.


Patchwork quilts! Memory brings back
the vision of the small child, seated on a
low stool beside memorable preceptress,
who instructed the weeping victim in the
polite mysteries of an "inner patch," while
urging her to remember the exact relation
of the letters of the alphabet. There is a
marvellous, though somewhat crude, art in
these bedspreads, made from the scraps of
cotton, and in some of the finer ones, their
genuine value given by the quilting.

London, May 19.--Escorted by members of Parliament, nearly 400 women suffragists representing organizations from all parts of the country, interviewed Premier Campbell Banerman at the Foreign Office to-day and presented their claims that women be allowed to vote. Only eight members of the numerous population were allowed to speak and in accordance with previous arrangement each speaker was limited to five minutes. But in the aggregate of 40 minutes the Premier heard about all there was to hear in favor of woman suffrage. The immediate grant of the woman's rights was the unanimous demand of the speakers, some of whom presented to the Premier their "minimum demands," claiming that immediate legislation allowing on women the right to vote was necessary and declaring that a promise to take the matter up at the next session of Parliament would not satisfy them.

One speaker menacingly declared that the women were prepared to sacrifice their lives in behalf of their demands.

The Premier smiled upon the strangely assorted gathering of women, including as it did ladies of title side by side with factory employees, and said he sympathized with the object of the population, but asked his visitors to be patient until the government granted extension of the franchise to women. The cause, he said, had made enormous strides of late years. Personally he believed that women were as well qualified as men and perhaps better to exercise the right to vote, and in his opinion, the deputation had made out a conclusive and irrefutable case.

Speaking for others, however, as well as himself, the Premier pointed out that it was necessary to preach the virtue of patience. Only harm would result if, because of his own sympathies and convictions, he gave a pledge regarding the time and method of achieving the object they had in view. No party or government was entirely united on the subject. He warned the women against indiscreet action which, he said, probably would check the flowing tide, and advised them to leave the matter confidently to the growing strength of their cause.

To the Editor:

I noticed somewhere recently—I
would not say positively that it was in
your columns—an article on the White
House which contained several mis-
statements.

In the first place it was stated the
White House was first occupied in
1909 and that its first occupant was
President Madison. The fact is, its
first occupant was President Adams,
who took up his residence there in
1800.

The original mansion was begun in
1792. In 1874 it was burned by the
British and rebuilt in 1818.

Another of the errors in the article
referred to was the statement that
ready-prepared paint is used on the
White House to make it beautifully
white.

I noticed this especially because I
have used considerable paint myself
and wondered that "canned" paint
should be used on such an important
building when all painters know that
pure white lead and linseed oil make
the best paint.

It so happened also that I knew
white lead and linseed oil—not ready
mixed paint—were used on the White
House, because I had just read a book
published by a firm of ready-mixed
paint manufacturers who also manu-
facture pure white lead. In that book
the manufacturers admitted that for
the White House nothing but the
best and purest of paint could be
used and said that their pure white
lead had been selected.

Above all, people, those who attempt
to write on historical subjects should
give us facts, even if it is only a date
or statement about wood, or brick,
or paint, or other building material.

Yours for truth,

The baseball season of 1905 has closed!

with Washington standing lower in the American League race than it did last year.

Why is this the case?

The answer is—lack of teamwork, another name for brains, and of properly equipped management.

Stupid Plays Were Rife.

Hard luck figures to some extent in the showing made by the team, but its final position can in no wise be blamed upon adverse fates. The team simply did not play up to the ability of the individual members, and at critical moments when a bit of coolness or ordinary backlot baseball strategy would have saved the day, the Nationals were not there with the goods. It is almost a safe bet that no team in either major league made so many stupid, inexcusable amateurish plays in the past season as did Washington, and that no team in either league so frequently violated the primary, fundamental rules of scientific baseball. Some of the instances were so raw that they brought derisive groans and heckles from the fans, and perhaps were not equaled by one of the organizations when competed for the District amateur championship.

Errors of omission cost Washington almost as much this season as the errors credited in the official scores. An analysis of the games by those who saw it playing at home and abroad shows game after game that was literally given away because the fielders became confused and did not throw the ball at all, or, if they did throw it, sent it to the wrong place.

Lack of Preconcerted Action.

There was an absolute lack of that harmony and preconcerted action between second, short, and third which was astonishing in a major league. In critical situations no one seemed to know what to do, each man acted on his own initiative and the consequence was that even umpires had to laugh at the ludicrous tangles which ensued. Receiving the ball from the catcher, handling blows into doubtful territory, solving problems that arose instantaneously and offered opportunities for brilliant strokes—it was all the same—the set-to-gether spirit and knowledge were missing. The number of instances in which second and shortstop failed to act in unison was almost sickening, while the methods of second, first, and pitcher in handling slight taps between first and second was equally bad. Nobody seemed to know what to do, and when he did, he did it wrong.

There was no guiding hand, no commanding voice to direct the work in a manner that would prevent the many errors. Bases were left uncovered, wild heaves were common, and collisions frequently imminent.

No Teamwork in Infield.

What was true of the infield was true of the outfield, especially in the matter of deciding who should take a fly in neutral territory, in the far gardens or in the short fields back of the bases. Infielders would sally into left center or right, attempting impossible catches of balls far beyond them, or perhaps stand still and look foolish while an outfielder ran in from the fence in a useless endeavor to nab a ball that would have been a catch for second or short, for instance.

It was disheartening, dispiriting, and discouraging, and the Washington pitchers cannot be blamed for many of their weird explosions because of the support they received.

Nationals Not Weak at Bat.

At bat Washington was not as weak as its final percentage of victories would indicate, but the teamwork in batting and base-running was little better than that in field. The man at the plate and the man on the bag had only vague notions of how to make the most of their opportunities. There was more or less sacrifice hitting and some good base-running by Anderson, Altiar, and one or two others, but the tactics were anticipated to a degree, the system was known to every club catcher in the league, and that they pilfered as many sacks as they did is a wonder of the national game. It was not a champion team, and champion form was not expected, but some of the base-running would have been a reproach to the South Texas League.

In connection with the work on the paths it may be said that Washington's coaching was enough to drive strong men to drink and women into hysterics. Occasionally it was strongly suggestive of that seen in a game between two brewery teams, where they open a fresh keg after every run. Time and again men were caught when a good coacher could have saved them, and almost as often they were left high and dry when they should have scored. A man is not put on the coaching line merely to bark at the opposing pitcher, cast insinuations upon the umpire, and yell with monotonous regularity, "Come on, old boy, get a good start!" He is there to serve as an additional pair of eyes for the runner and to direct his movements according to the highest and most complicated developments of the sport, but if anybody in the Washington club knew that answer he failed to hold an inkling, and tell the teacher.

Pitching staff Was Fair.

Concerning its pitchers, Washington had some good luck and some bad. Patten, who was a failure last year, was a decided success this season, and did much to prevent the showing from being worse than it was. Falkenberg was erratic and fortunate. He was slugged freely and hard in games in which Washington would suddenly, after a week of poor hitting, come to life and pound the opposing twirler to a jelly. This happened so often, he became a joke.

La suma que el éxito de esa reclamación traería a nuestro Tesoro, no es nada despreciable, como puede verse. Son cien mil dollars que ha dejado il de las manos la incuria de la congregación.

Y ahora que está en Nueva York el Tesorero, designado con el Auditor y el Attorney para recoger el sobrante del empréstito, no estaría de más recordarle que está obligado a conseguir que la importante suma procedente de la fianza evaporada, se haga efectiva de una vez.

Entonces fue que la opinión hizo exteriores sus inquietudes y alarmas.

La congregación estaba obligada a perseguir por todos los medios la entrega de la cuantiosa suma, desaparecida en virtud.

of the board of health in an address be-
fore the county and city health officers
of the state.


DR.. Crumbine told of experiments he
had made on dogs, and with the results
as his text he urged that the state board
of health limit the use of preservatives
to food stuffs that are to be shipped
long distances during the summer
months. DIR. Crumbine said that on May
! he took three dogs of the same age.
Every morning he fed each one half a
pint of fresh lean meat, at noon each
pint of milk and at night each dog had
another half pint of meat. The meat
was fresh, without bones, and was not
scraps. The food for one day as treated
with one per cent solution of benzoate.
For the second one per cent solution
of borax was used. The third dog was
fed untreated milk and meat.


Within two weeks the benzoate dog
became cross and refused to have any
thing to do with the others. 1t lost its
appetite and in six weeks had gained
only three pounds in weight. The borax
dog did net become cross. but within
ten days its general health declined and
it refused to drink the boated milk. In
four weeks it had to be coaxed to eat
meat even tasteless boracic acid. The
dog gained one pound in weight in six
weeks but became listless. The dog that
had been fed untreated meat, gained in
weight an average of one pound a week
during the test and at no time did it
become listless or lose its appetite.

Philadelphia, Aug. 17.—With a warrant out for his arrest, charging him with embezzling $500 which was to have been used in paying off church mortgage, Rev. George H. Culley, pastor of the Sixth Christian Church, is missing. Efforts to locate the fugitive clergyman have thus far failed, though he is believed by his congregation to be with his wife and child in New York.

The money which Mr. Culley is accused of embezzling was raised by Mrs. John Beveridge, one of his congregation, who mortgaged her home and entrusted the $500 to the pastor. Bender, secretary of the church, was instructed to swear out a warrant for the missing pastor's arrest.

Special to The Times Dispatch.
WASHINGTON, August 20.—An amazing condition of affairs is alleged in a report made to Secretary Hitchcock, of the Interior Department by Special Agent Frank Churchill concerning the management of the schools and reindeer in Alaska by the Rev. Sheldon Jackson, the Commissioner of Education for that territory, and author of the scheme to make the natives of Alaska self-supporting by the introduction of reindeer into their country. Trappers OF the Northwest Included

in General Prosperity.

The many trappers operating in northern Minnesota will reap a rich harvest during the present winter. This sidesweep of the general wave of prosperity that has rolled over the land means many comforts, even luxuries, in the log cabins of scores of sturdy settlers in the wilds of the northern country, who are mainly dependent upon their traps during the cold months for a livelihood.

The settlers and professionals in the country directly tributary to Duluth look for the most part to mink, marten and otter to make their trapping operations profitable and the pelts of these little animals at present command a higher price than at any time during the past 50 years, though there has been a decided slump in the prices paid for furs from the black, blue and silver fox, which bring only $50 each now, where a year or two ago they were as high as $500 apiece.

Last winter $3.50 was considered a good price for a mink pelt and it wasn't more than a season or two back that $3.50 was the highest paid for a single pelt OF this kind. Now a choice raw mink fur will bring $1 and a marten pelt from $15 to $40, where $5 or $1 was paid last winter. An otter skin is worth $500 just as it comes from the trapper's hands, which is away above any price paid for more than thirty years. Quite a few fisher are caught through northern Minnesota and these are worth from $15 to $50. Beaver are very scarce and are worth from $1 to $50 each.

The highest prices paid for furs will also prove a boon to the Minnesota Indians or such of them at least as have any business ability. A great many of the Indians trap during the winter, but the trouble with the majority of them is that they do not know the value of their catch and are likely to sell $50 otter pelt for $1 or $5 and a $1 mink for $1, or perhaps a pint of whisky. The white man is well aware of this fact and some agents make it their business during the winter to do nothing but buy furs from the Indians, selling them later at a handsome margin of profit.

nent father. He has the same clear-cut
finely chiseled face, the keen eye, the firm,
small mouth, the inevitable monocle and
the ever-present orchid in his coat lapel.

great men cannot have a great son, for
Mr. Austen is exceedingly great in many
respects. He has been the best Chancellor
of the Exchequer that this country has
known for many generations. He was
an ideal Postmaster General, and while he falls
short of his father's exceptional ability as
a fighting man in debate, he is still so far
in front of his contemporaries that he may
be called first-class. Aside from this, he is
modest, sedate, studious, industrious and
considerate; and his father simply adores
him. It is almost pathetic to watch the
elder statesman when the younger is on his
feet in the House of Commons.


The old warrior, scarred by many fights
with the great men of the Victorian parlia-
ments, sits up straight, never allowing his
eyes to leave the adored object. "I con-
gratulate my right honorable friend the
member for Edgbaston," says Mr. Chamber-

never mentioned in the House except by
the speaker when he wishes a member to
know that he is in disgrace), and Mr. Aus-
ten refers to his parent "My right hon-
orable friend the member for West Birming-
ham."


There are people here who believe that a
man's usefulness as a politician is impaired
by marriage, and that the member for Edg-
baston will not be so great a man after the
ceremony at the church, but I am inclined
to scoff at the idea. There are and have
been so many great men in politics whose
married life belies it. Mr. Gladstone's wife
was responsible for much of his power, for
she looked after him, arranged his engage-
ments and generally sponsored him. Lord
Beaconsfield, the success of successes, was
married, so were Palmerston and Salisbury.

the experience of Lord Melbourne to
Charles James Fox, to Mr. Parnell, to Mr.

liamentary life, like journalism, certainly
takes a man from his home circle more than
is usual with men who live a less exciting
and exacting life. Men who never reach
home until the midnight hour has long
since gone, and the gray dawn is turning
out the street lights, cannot expect to lead
carpet slipper life, unless, mayhap, they
intend to neglect their duties.

The Chicago Glee club, without
any doubt, stands among the best
male quartets this country has ever
produced. The fact that every voice
is peculiarly adapted to the part it
assumes and that the membership of
the club has been so long unchanged,
combine to produce this high degree
of excellence. The volume of the
voices is such as to fill the largest
auditorium, while pianissimo pas
sages are so fine and harmonious as
to hold the audience in breathless
attention. The repertoire of the
club is very extensive and comprises
the best of all classes of music
written for male voices. Many of
the selections used by the club have
been written or arranged especially
for it.


Mr.. Dixon has been reading with
the club for several seasons. His
work is distinctly along the line of
representations. His presentation of
character types, such as portrayed
by James Whitcomb Riley, is par
ticularly faithful. A thorough con-
troll of facial expression and an
intimate knowledge Of his subject
enables him to bring before the
audience the character true to life.
These readings are strong feature
of the program.


The club offers a decidedly novel
feature in the form of a quartet of
slide trombones. The trombone is
conceded to be the king" of wind
instruments, and the effect produced
by the four quite approaches in
sweetness and volume the quality
and power of a pipe organ. With
these instruments supplementing the
male quartet, the club is able to
present a varied and artistic even
ing. They will appear at the opera
house Jan. 9th, benefit of public
library.

DYING On Train.

Dublin, Ga. March 31.—On the
Wrightsville and Tennille passenger
train at Lovejoy, a pistol fell from the
pocket of Deputy Sheriff John A. Wal-
den, and was fired. The ball entered
the right eye of Mrs. Joeena Crabb,
piercing the brain and causing her
death in about an hour.

Mrs. Crabb was in the custody of the
deputy, and a man by the name of J.
N. Joiner was, it is said, trying to
take her from him. Joiner had Mrs.
Crabb's satchel, and was going to the
door of the coach with Mr. Walden
caught the satchel and endeavored to
prevent Joiner from taking it. In the
scuffle, the pistol fell from the pocket
of the officer, with the above result.

There were number of people on
the car, who testify that the killing
was an accident, and was unavoidable.

Among the passengers were Superintendent
Holloman, of the Wrightsville
and Tennille road, and Presiding Elder
Mathews of this district. They ex-
onerate the deputy.

Mrs. Crabb was arrested in Dublin
on a warrant sworn out by Mrs. Wyatt,
mother of the woman, who charged her
with deserting her children. She was
arrested on Wednesday by Sheriff
Prince, who placed her in charge of
Walden, to be carried to Meadows.

The woman died shortly after the
train reached Meadows. Joiner asked
that she be placed in his custody, even
after it was seen that she was dying,
but the officers refused to do this.

The satchel which Joiner tried to
take from the train contained a pistol
and a box of cartridges.

No blame is attached to the officer,
who was simply endeavoring to do his
duty.

The latest directory of the Delaware &
Atlantic Telegraph and Telephone Co. for
the Wilmington district, issued under date
Of May, 1906, has been visited with many
hot and hostile criticisms, by reason Of its
highly unsatisfactory character and inn
perfections Of arrangement and work.
manship.


Prominent among the defects is the
exceedingly close printing, resulting in an
economy of space that has produced irri-
tating results. The lines Of numbers and
names are set close together, a defect
which would be serious even with the
employment Of larger type, but which,
combined with the small body Of the type
in which the book is set, makes the expert
ence Of searching out desired name very
trying TO eyes and brain, and highly con
ducive to aggravating mistakes when the
searcher is in a hurry.


Another serious defect il the setting Of
the numbers in light-iace type, while the
names are set in black-face. To those
who have occasion for frequent calls this
defect is particularly aggravating. The
numbers should be even more conspicu-
GUS than the names, as was the rule in
previous issues Of this directory all but
one Of which we're so satisfactory in char
acter as TO provoke not the slightest un-
favorable comment.


The typographical appearance Of the
book is the limit Of ugliness. In addition
TO the unfavorable effect Of the crowded
lines, scarcely a page can be found in
which the alignment Of the names is
straight. On most Of them it is as
crooked as the proverbial dogs hind
leg" Nor are typographical errors in
frequent. One prominent institution in
this city, which has a large service, is
put down as 966, whereas its correct
number is 996 The annoyance to which
the concern and its customers and also
the real 966 are subjected by this error in
figures may be readily imagined. An
other conspicuous typographical error is
found In the list Of subscribers TO the
exchange at Belle Haven, Va.-the

where Nassawadox, on the New York,
Philadelphia & Norfolk Railroad, is per-
sistently spelled Massawadox. How
many other typographical blunders might
be revealed by a critical scrutiny Of the
pages is a matter Of conjecture.


Taken in its entirety, the directory is
not only very unsatisfactory, but falls
far below the standard which is Justly
demanded by the extent and Importance
of the telephone business of the Whining

The musical enthusiasm of Hadar is growing apace. The two bands of the little town of sixty-three inhabitants now have combined membership of fifty-two. The 7-year-old son of H. Hollyfield had his leg broken in a wheel of one of the Fair store delivery wagons yesterday afternoon. Just after school the wagon was going up Third street and a crowd of boys, in which was the Hollyfield boy, ran after it and tried to crowd on. Lewis, who was driving the wagon, heard the cries of the boy and backed up so as to free the boy. Local grave diggers, especially those
at Odd Fellows and Fairview cemet-
cries where hard digging at a certain
depth is factor will be very glad to
learn that the State Department of
Health has prescribed new regulations
for the burying of human bodies in the
cemeteries of Pennsylvania'to meet the
objections, which have been raised to
the original regulations adopted re-
Gently by Commissioner Dixon.


The order sent out by DR.. Dixon and
which went into effect on January 1st
provided that the distance from the
top Of the box containing the coffin or
casket be seven feet from the natural
surface of the ground. This gave the
grave total depth Of about nine feet.
Where the ground afforded easy dig
ging to the depth named there could
probably be little objection to the new
| regulation. But the fact in the begin
ming was lost sight of that in many
cemeteries nine feet would carry the
l
ing the use of explosives before the
proper depth could be attained. The
new ruling was especially hard on
the grave digger at Odd Fellows ceme-
terry, where at a depth of some seven
feet shelly rock is encountered. At
the Fairview cemetery conditions are
nearly as bad, at the same depth de-
posit of hard pan being encountered,
which makes digging difficult.


The grave diggers naturally protest
ed against being obliged to sink graves
to such an unusual depth in the face
of such obstacles as existed. The un-
dertakers insisted upon carrying out
the letter Of the law and the grave
diggers did their best to comply. Only
a few funerals have occurred since
January LIST and what success the reg
ulations later on would have met with
had it not been for the new order it
would be hard to say. A man Of aver
age stature by adding a yard to his
height can form an idea of the depth
of grave required. In the case of an
infants grave to comply with the reg
ulation became impracticable or a
physical impossibility.


The new regulation prescribed pro-
vides that except by special permission
from the department no interment of
any human body shall be made in any
public or private burial ground unless
the distance from the top of the box
containing the coffin or casket be at
least five feet from the natural surface
of the ground, except where solid rock
or water may be encountered.


| Then the distance from the top of
the box containing the coffin or casket
shall not be less than four feet from
the natural surface of the ground and
with the further exception that still
born children and children less than
four years old dead of any disease 9th
er than anthrax, cholera, diphtheria,
small pox, scarlet fever. tetanus and
typhoid fever shall be buried at such
depth that the top of the box contain
ing the coffin or casket be not less than
three and one-half feet from the natur-
al surface of the ground.

Rarely has the story of the life and death of a dumb animal come so near to the elements of human tragedy as the dog's tale of Brodie, the faithful mascot of the Delancey street station house, as mentioned in the wireless despatch printed above. Brodie really jumped from the Williamsburg Bridge only a few days ago, but in the cold words of the news message there is no reference to the causes that prompted the heartbroken animal's frightful leap. If the policeman could have interpreted the expression of weakness in Brodie, with a big black head and bits of chestnut burrs concealed in the wavy hair of her tail, in the bright sunlight of last Monday forenoon, he would have learned that no matter what the cold, scientific Thompson Setons may say, Brodie had deliberately planned suicide, with no wish for anything but a peace of oblivion, with no hope for fame and a saloon on the Bowery with John L. Sullivan's photograph in evening clothes in the window and the diamond belt back of the free lunch.

She had dragged herself, homeless and alone, painfully up the bridge approach and hour after hour had gazed wanly over the roofs of the city. Smoke was curling cheerfully from many a housetop, and the shouts of little children throwing Kinney bricks down at passing automobiles came to Brodie's ears, but there was none to throw a brick at her. She sighed and cowered against the railing, waiting for night to fall so that she might crawl up to some basement window and watch the merry household trimming a Christmas tree, perhaps, while she shivered in the cold night.

Some might say that Brodie was attrabilious, but there were days when she was the happiest dog in the Gouverneur Hospital district. Then one day her first born was skinned by a vivisectionist before her very eyes, and before the first stitch had been taken to replace the skin in the interest of science, Brodie's spirit had been broken beyond repair. She wandered out of the laboratory in a daze and never again was known to skip and romp. Since then she had wandered the streets until she became the hollow eyed, sunken cheeked wreck that was picked up on Delaney street by Policeman Otto Nickly on Monday evening after her terrible leap.

Tenderly the policeman carried Brodie over to the Delaney street station, where there are cells. When she heard the cries that greeted her entrance, Brodie cowered and pressed closer to the policeman till her bedraggled coat and Otto's mustache were lost in each other. It took the poor thing a long time to realize that the cries were of gladness and that she was being welcomed by those who had seen sorrow and could understand it.

"We'll make her the station house mascot," Otto cried Sergt. Shanahan, clapping his hands gleefully. "Every fire house has a mascot that carries in the morning paper, and when a fireman gets hurt the mascot runs into the flames and tries to drag him out. Then they don't eat anything for days and days, but stand in front of Bellevue crying till the fireman gets well. I see it in the papers every month. We'll call him Brodie because of his jump and maybe he'll get to do things like other mascots before we get transferred."

But Brodie began to perform her duties. The very night she had been in the station house less than half an hour when Fritz, the meat waiter of Hanabe's restaurant in Grand street, came in with a platter containing a steak and a charlotte russo for the sergeant's evening meal. When Sergt. Shanahan merely saluted the steak as it was being carried past, and then turned to his profession again, Brodie looked worried and tried to drag the platter out of Fritz's hand so that she could carry it to his desk.

The sergeant misinterpreted Brodie's thoughtfulness and immediately yelled to the reserves to raise a dinner fund for the dog. Patrolman Henry Hadlick was appointed the entertainment committee and he soon rounded up six cents, of which Capt. Martin Handy contributed four cents. Hadlick ran out to Simon Smolinsky's delicatessen and came back with more actual food that Brodie had seen for a month. The mascot ate the ham and the salt herring with a relish and toyed long with the cheese, letting it roll away from her while she seemed to be watching something else, and when the cheese had almost reached the door, jumping upon it, to the great delight of her new friends.

And then when she had eaten even the cheese and the station had turned its attention to pinochle, Brodie, still anxious to show her gratitude, slipped out to where the sergeant's steak was growing cold at a corner table of the lounging room and tried to carry it to the sergeant. But as she jumped over the railing to lay the steak at Sergt. Shanahan's feet, the steak, unfortunately, slipped down the faithful dog's throat.

Late Monday night or early Tuesday morning the mascot awoke still hungry and began to nose among the snoring policemen in the dormitory for something unnecessary to her benefactors which would fill the internal vacuum. She changed upon Sergt. Mike Wall's human plug hat and reasoned at once that the hat was of next to no use to a uniformed policeman who was a utilitarian. Brodie merely nibbled at the outer crust of the hat tentatively for a few seconds and then turned her attention to a long row of wide shoes. She choked on Doorman Julie Leck's rubber heel and as the cops were awakened by her coughing and grasped the situation slowly, the faithful mascot was presented with a number of pairs of shoes immediately.

perhaps just as unworthy when he said,
"We have left all and followed thee,
what shall we have?" Giving in expecta-

sacrifice will suggest its own correlative,
namely, compensation. "What shall we
have?" is a legitimate question, but must
be kept in its proper place. Christ sought
to place in the human soul a moral dy-
namic of love to God and man, which,

acter, they bowed at the shrine of Mam-
mon. Christ stigmatized riches as a hin-
drance to entering the kingdom of heaven.

observing faithfully the principles of
Christian righteousness, is less likely to
be overcome with covetousness. His prin-
ciples will prevent it. Many followers of
Christ have grown rich and lost nothing of
his Christian character, but have splendidly
enlarged his career of usefulness.

saving. But the person who starts out in
life bent on making money, in whom the
moral dynamic of love to God and man is

ings, you can only make so much, you will
only make the ten. Thus you will not
only maintain character, but increase it,
and the treasure of character is one of
heaven's brightest gems, and the reward
is for those with kindred characters in
time and in eternity.

application of these principles in these
times. Perhaps few people are held in
greater contempt than the men who were
recently proved thieves and robbers, con-

difference is against them. The recent

strongest hold of all upon his life.

hue and cry of certain politicians and

that conduct is immoral which contra-
venes any God-given precept. God's
standard is high, but the measure of peo-
ple's character is the measure of their
growth, and not their increase in wealth.

principles—the principle of living, laboring

Oregon. In one day's hunting last
summer, there were 4,000 pheasants
killed by hunters in that state. At one
time the pheasants became so tame
that the farmers thought they were
injuring the crops. The state legisla-
ture therefore removed all restrictions
from killing them, and a general
slaughter was started for the purpose of
determination. Later the farmers
discovered that it wasn't the pheasants
after all that were injuring the crops,
and the killing of the pheasants was
restricted to certain months. That is
the way things stand now out there.

We now have ninety-two pheasants
at the hatchery at Pratt. They have
all been sent to me from Oregon. I
have bought all there are for sale out
there now, and have contracted for
1,000 more next summer. I want to
get about 5,000 birds altogether, and
scatter them throughout the state. This,
with what we can hatch at the state
hatchery, ought to enable us to thor-
oughly stock the state within a few
years.

are not migratory. They get into the
timber or brush, and keep out of the
snow in that way. During the winter
they live on seeds of weeds, kaffir corn
shocks, etc. Their habits are very much
like those of the quail.

fatal thing to the pheasants are their
long tails. Their tails drag on the
ground and as it is their habit to roost
in the snow they sometimes are caught
in a thaw and freeze, and their tails are
frozen into the snow. This holds them
prisoner sometimes until they starve to
death."

In the face of the assembling of hostile Parliament, it is apparent that the Emperor and the Court are trying desperately to obtain the good will of the representatives by all manner of pacific assurances. Now that Count Witte has fallen, a distinct impression is being fostered that he was dismissed because he was too reactionary, and it is announced that the changes in the fundamental laws, of which he is charged with being the author, will be withdrawn. This promise is a great victory for the Liberals, and accounts in measure for the optimistic tone of M. Milukof's speech in the Constitutional Democratic convention.

M. Schwanebach's statement to-day that it is the sincere intention of Emperor Nicholas to give to the people representative institutions, and that he has intention of dissolving Parliament, is another sign of the government's desire to avoid a conflict. The prospects of the first Parliament achieving something have suddenly frightened. If the government is sincere, however, the Goremykin Cabinet will be only a temporary ministry, which will be succeeded by a Cabinet representing the dominant party. It is inconceivable that the opposition in Parliament will make a truce on any other basis. Already in the congress of the Constitutional Democrats the extreme wing has expressed itself in favor of war.

A sharp fight is foreshadowed against the efforts of the moderate leaders to prevent the adoption of a detailed programme, their plan being to keep the direction of party tactics in the hands of a central committee which they control.

Schwanebach, former Minister of Agriculture, Controller of the Empire in the new Cabinet and Premier Goremykin's chief lieutenant, sent for the Associated Press's correspondent to-day and requested in behalf of the new Premier that it be announced to the United States and to the world in the following official note that the new ministry does not mean reaction:

There is no intention of dissolving Parliament. Naturally, unforeseen circumstances may arise as in any government, which may force such an unhappy event, but we do not anticipate such a misfortune, as the majority of the members of Parliament are lovers of their country, and we do not believe that they are desirous of forcing a conflict.
